background.definition: A cataract is a degradation of the optical quality of the crystalline lens. Most cataract development is related to aging.

list.listitem: Cataract is the leading cause of blindness, responsible for up to 48% blindness in the world. With the aging of the population, the prevalence of visually significant cataracts will increase.
In the United States, between 1996 and 2000, Medicare spending on cataract surgery was $3 billion per year.
Cataract surgery per eye costs between $2000 and $4500, which compares favorably with other common surgical procedures per quality-adjusted life-year gained.
The likelihood of cataracts increases with age, sun exposure, and comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus.
Cataracts may be congenital.
They are common post-vitrectomy.
Long-term corticosteroid use increases the risk as well.

As the human lens ages, the nucleus undergoes compression and hardening (nuclear sclerosis); as the lens proteins change, they become yellow and then brown. The optical quality of the lens declines due to light scatter, increasing aberrations, and loss of accommodation.
Long-term exposure to even low levels of ultraviolet-B (UV-B) from sun exposure is associated with an increased risk of cortical and posterior subcapsular cataracts.
Cataract is a common cause of visual impairment in patients with diabetes.
Long-term use of corticosteroids, inhaled or systemic, is associated with an increased risk for developing cataracts, especially in children.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force reports that there is insufficient evidence to recommend screening to improve outcomes in older adults. The American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends routine eye examination every 1 to 3 years for patients between the ages of 55 years and 64 years and every 1 to 2 years for patients older than 65 years. A Cochrane review concluded that there is no evidence that community-based screening of asymptomatic older people results in improvements in vision.C
Patients should avoid tobacco use, wear sunglasses to protect from UV light, control their diabetes and hypertension, minimize use of corticosteroids, and avoid trauma. B

The highest quality evidence does not support a benefit from nutritional supplementation in preventing or delaying progression of cataracts. Therefore, treatment with supplements is not recommended. A
Large RCTs have demonstrated that anti-oxidant vitamins (beta-carotene, Vitamin C, Vitamin E) do not prevent cataracts.A
While statins are associated with a decreased risk of developing cataracts, no clinical trials have confirmed their role in prevention. B
No single test adequately describes the impact of cataract on visual function or determines the indication for cataract surgery. C
Visual function questionnaires, a complete ophthalmic examination, and an assessment for functional impairment under different light conditions help to determine the indication for surgery. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Corneal epithelial staining, decreased tear breakup time, irregular corneal topography
Cell or flare, cystoid macular edema
Epiretinal membrane, abnormal fluorescein angiography or optical coherence tomography
Optic pallor, visual field abnormalities, abnormal magnetic resonance imaging

list.listitem: Patients generally present with complaints of difficulty driving, reading, watching television, recognizing faces, or enjoying recreational pursuits. On occasion, the complaint may relate to the patient's occupation, particularly in the transportation, medical, and legal fields because of the high demands on visual function.
Inquire about the functional significance of impaired vision with reference to the patient's activities.

Because vision depends on luminance, glare, and contrast, ask the patient about environmental conditions that either improve or degrade vision (eg, "Do you have increasing trouble reading road signs at night when there are oncoming headlights?").

To objectively assess for functional impairment under different light conditions, the ophthalmologist can assess for a decline in patients' best-corrected visual acuity, reduced contrast sensitivity, and reduced visual acuity under glare conditions.
Lens opacities are best characterized by slit-lamp examination. These opacities are generally graded using the Lens Opacities Classification System III.

The functional status of the macula and optic nerve must be assessed to ascertain that other pathology does not explain the loss of vision (eg, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and ischemic optic neuropathy).
If cataract is suspected, a visual function questionnaire can help delineate the degree of functional vision impairment.

Physical examination should include a determination of the refractive status of each eye and the best-corrected visual acuity, as well as a complete ophthalmic examination including the pupils, ocular motility, and ocular adnexa; a slit-lamp examination; and a dilated funduscopic examination.

Consider the following tests when decreased visual function is not explained by reduced high-contrast visual acuity: brightness acuity testing (visual acuity under glare conditions), contrast sensitivity testing (using sine wave gratings over a range of spatial frequencies and contrast levels), and potential acuity testing (to determine the functional status of the macula).
Extracapsular cataract surgery by phacoemulsification with IOL implantation provides safe and effective treatment for patients with cataract. A
Innovations in IOL design have increased quality of life for patients desiring independence from glasses after surgery. A
Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs prevent and treat cystoid macular edema postoperatively. B

Extracapsular cataract surgery by phacoemulsification with IOL implantation provides safe and effective treatment for patients with cataract. It is indicated that when visual function no longer meets the patient's needs, cataract surgery provides a reasonable likelihood of improvement. This is an individualized decision. Indications for cataract surgery for the second eye are the same as for the first eye.
AAO guidelines note that refractive cataract surgery can reduce a patient's dependence on eyeglasses or contact lenses.
A systematic review found that multifocal IOLs are an effective option for patients desiring "spectacle independence" and good vision at a range of distances.

Complication rates for cataract surgery are low. In a meta-analysis of 90 published studies of cataract surgery outcomes, less than 0.5% of eyes developed endophthalmitis or bullous keratopathy; less than 1% developed retinal detachments; and less than 2% developed dislocation or malposition of the IOL, elevated intraocular pressure, or clinically apparent cystoid macular edema.
There is no difference in outcomes or complications between outpatient and inpatient surgery for cataract. Cost is lower with outpatient surgery.

A Cochrane review concluded that both Sub-Tenon's anesthesia and topical anesthesia are similarly effective. A second review concluded that peribulbar and retrobulbar anesthesia are also similarly effective.
The incidence of capsular opacification and the need for YAG laser capsulotomy ranges from 3% to 17% of eyes 3 years after surgery and varies with the type of IOL implant material and design.

All patients undergoing cataract surgery should have a history and physical examination to assess risk factors for undergoing the planned anesthesia and sedation. Most patients undergoing cataract surgery do not benefit from routine ECG and laboratory testing.
A Cochrane review concluded that routine preoperative testing prior to cataract surgery does not improve outcomes.

In a study of nearly 20,000 patients undergoing cataract surgery, there was no significant difference in the risk of ocular hemorrhage between patients who continued and patients who discontinued aspirin, and there were no ocular hemorrhage at all among warfarin users. There was also no difference in the risk of myocardial infarction, hemorrhagic cystitis, myocardial ischemia, stroke, and deep vein thrombosis.
There are no randomized trials to demonstrate the benefit of cataract surgery post-vitrectomy.

A small study of 82 eyes found that cataract surgery improved visual acuity when indicated in patients with wet macular degeneration, but there was a suggestion of more cystoid macular edema in the intervention group.
There is not enough data to determine the long term benefit of cataract surgery in patients with age-related macular degeneration.
Topical NSAIDs reduce early post-operative cystoid macular edema, but long-term effects are not known.
Immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery is non-inferior to delayed sequential bilateral cataract surgery and is cost-effective.
No supplements have been found to be effective in treating cataracts.
Early cataract will cause a change in refractive error, which can sometimes be managed with a change in the spectacle or contact lens prescription.
Patients who develop posterior capsule opacification may require YAG laser capsulotomy. This complication appears to be less common in patients given IOLs with a sharp (posterior) optic edge.
Endophthalmitis (postoperative infection) requires immediate management with vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal antibiotics or vitrectomy.
Cystoid macular edema may be prevented and treated by the use of topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.
Patients with dry eye following cataract surgery can be treated with artificial tears or diquafosol.

Most patients should be examined within 24 hours following cataract surgery. Low-risk patients without signs or symptoms of possible complications following small-incision cataract surgery should be seen within 48 hours. C
In general, there is rapid visual rehabilitation, with improvement in visual acuity by the first postoperative day. C

Contemporary cataract surgery has an excellent success rate, both in terms of improving visual acuity and enhancing subjective visual function. More than 90% of otherwise healthy eyes achieve a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/40 or better. A

Management of congenital or developmental cataract in children differs markedly from the management of cataract in the adult eye, primarily because of amblyopia and secondarily because of the increased challenges posed by inflammation, posterior capsular opacification, and growth of the eye. Primary implantation of an IOL at the time of cataract surgery may be considered.
